tagline.text: A lime-and-coral Ivatan stone house built in 1887 that still stands in Ivana

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Radiwan, Ivana, Batanes, along the national road on Batan Island

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–1,700 (per person; visit registration, tricycle or South Batan tour, excluding flights and lodging)

children.text: The House of Dakay is a traditional Ivatan stone house built in 1887 in Ivana, Batanes. Its thick walls of coral, stone and lime and its cogon-grass roof have withstood fierce typhoons and earthquakes for more than a hundred years. It is the place in South Batan where you can see Ivatan architecture up close.

The House of Dakay (Vahay ni Dakay in Ivatan) is an old stone house in Ivana, in the south of Batan Island, the main island of Batanes. On the map it stands along the national road in Barangay Radiwan, Ivana, and it often appears in the afternoon part of the South Batan loop heading south from Basco. Several sources describe it as built in 1887 and rank it among the oldest surviving stone houses in Batanes. However, some sources give the year as 1877, so the exact year differs slightly by source. Ivana had a population of about 1,368 in the 2024 census, making it the smallest town in Batanes and the second least populated in the whole Philippines. The barangay of Radiwan, where the house stands, has about 381 residents according to Wikipedia, so even just walking its quiet roads gives you a feel for island life.

The house is known as a "sinandumparan" style home, which Ivatan people have long built. According to accounts, coral washed in from the shore and stones common in Ivana were bound together with lime, and the walls are up to 1 m thick and sometimes reinforced with wood. The roof is made of thick cogon grass laced onto the rafters, then covered by a rope net tied to stones set in the ground so that strong winds cannot lift it away. The door is small and narrow and faces east or northeast, and the windows are small squares cut into three walls only. It is practical wisdom for surviving on an island of fierce winds and frequent typhoons.

The story of this house is tied to earthquakes. Sources say that in the strong earthquake of September 13, 1918 only five houses in Ivana survived and this was one of them. The same sources say it also withstood the magnitude 7 earthquake of July 16, 2000. The house is named after an ancestor, Jose "Dakay" Estrella, and sources differ on who first built it, naming Luisa or Elena Estrella. The Estrella family is still said to look after the house, and an elderly Florestida Estrella (known as Lola Ida) is reported to live there and welcome visitors.

This guide is for travelers who tour South Batan from Basco for a day and want to see an Ivatan stone house up close. The house is not a museum but a home where someone lives, so the way you enter and the fees differ by source. A 2019 article said to register at the registration desk beside Mahatao Church and pay about ₱50 per person, while another source describes giving a donation to the owner. Check the guidance before you visit and look around quietly. The inside has almost no furniture and a sign that explains the house's history. Some descriptions link it to a UNESCO list, but I could not confirm this, so treat it as a reference only.

The thick walls of coral and stone from the sea, bound with lime, are the heart of this house. Walls up to 1 m thick are Ivatan wisdom for blocking fierce winds and earthquakes. Look with your eyes rather than your hands.

The roof is thick laced cogon grass, and one source says it is re-thatched every 20–30 years. Notice also how the roof is covered with a rope net tied down to stones. It is a device to keep the roof from blowing away in typhoons.
The door is small and narrow and faces east or northeast, and the windows are small squares on three walls only. It is described as a structure to reduce strong wind. Watch your head when entering.

In the September 13, 1918 earthquake only five houses in Ivana are said to have survived and this was one. There is also an explanation that it withstood the July 2000 magnitude 7 earthquake. This story can reportedly be read on the sign as well.
The kitchen and toilet are said to have been built as separate buildings from the main house. You can see an old way of life that kept fire and sanitation apart.

The house has been kept by the Estrella family, and an elderly Florestida Estrella is known to live there. Because it is a residence, ask permission before taking photos and find out how to receive guidance and give a donation.

blocks.title: A stop on the South Batan loop

children.text: The House of Dakay sits between Ivana town and the Honesty Coffee Shop, so it fits naturally into the afternoon route. After seeing Chawa Viewdeck, Mahatao Church and Tayid Lighthouse, continue to it in the afternoon.

items.title: Full-day South Batan route
items.subtitle: From the viewdeck to the stone house

children.text: Set out south from Basco and see Chawa Viewdeck in Mahatao as the first stop.
Visit Mahatao Church, Tayid Lighthouse, Diura Fishing Village and Racuh a Payaman in turn.
Have lunch at a restaurant in Mahatao or near Vayang.
Pass through Imnajbu, Alapad and Uyugan and continue toward Ivana.
Look over the stone house at the House of Dakay and listen to the owner's guidance.
Rest at the nearby Honesty Coffee Shop (an unmanned café) and return to Basco.
You cover many places in one day, so the schedule is tight. Leave slack so you are back in Basco before dark.
Go from Basco to Radiwan Port in Ivana. Boats to Sabtang leave in the morning.
Cross from Radiwan Port to Sabtang Island and look around the stone-house villages.
Take the return boat before the afternoon waves get rough.
Back in Ivana, look around the House of Dakay.

Boats to Sabtang usually leave around 6-7 AM and the return boat usually leaves around 1-2 PM; trips can be cancelled depending on sea conditions, so confirm the return boat early. Check the exact schedule locally.
Take a domestic flight from Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila to Basco Airport (BSO). Wikipedia says PAL Express operates the Manila route.
Small turboprop aircraft are used and flights are often cancelled in bad weather, so leave extra days in your schedule.
Round-trip fares vary greatly by season, and examples of about ₱10,000–20,000 have been reported.
There are reports that the pre-registration procedure for visiting Batanes has changed, so check provincial government announcements before you leave.
From Basco to Ivana you travel along the national road to the south. A South Batan tricycle tour was listed in a 2018 trip report at about
for two, and a group tour at about
per person.
It is convenient to be introduced to a van or tricycle driver and a guide through your lodging.

Boats to Sabtang Island leave from Radiwan Port in Ivana early in the morning (about 6-7 AM), and for a day trip you are told to take the return boat, which usually leaves around 1-2 PM. Departures depend on the Coast Guard's wave-condition check.
The House of Dakay and Radiwan Port are both in the Ivana area, so they combine well in one day.

Wikivoyage describes the best time for Batanes as the dry season of roughly March–June, when winds and waves calm down. In this period road closures and cancellations are less likely, so a South Batan loop is easier. Basco is known to get the most rain in August–September, and June–July are the hottest months.
The stone house is built to withstand both rain and wind, but roads and travel are strongly affected by weather. In typhoon season getting around may be difficult, so leave slack in your schedule.

There is almost no lodging near the House of Dakay, and most travelers stay in Basco town and visit on a day tour. There are small lodgings in Ivana and Mahatao as well. Wikivoyage advises that Basco is the only place on Batan with banks, so bring plenty of cash.

The nearby "Honesty Coffee Shop" is described as an unmanned shop. One trip report explains that you buy drinks, noodles, snacks and souvenirs, put the money in a box and write it in the journal. It shows the honesty of the Ivatan people, so follow the prices and the journal system. Eat other meals in Basco town or at restaurants in Mahatao.
The stone house is a residence. Ask permission before taking photos, keep your voice down, and do not touch or lean on the house.
There is guidance that visit registration is required, so first check local instructions such as the registration desk beside Mahatao Church. Amounts can change.
Cases of giving a donation to the owner as thanks are described. Prepare small cash.
A South Batan loop covers many places in a day, so the afternoon is tight. Plan to start with Chawa Viewdeck and see Ivana in the afternoon.
When looking at the cogon roof and lime walls up close, photos change with the direction of the light. Afternoon light shows the texture of the walls well.
If you combine it with the Sabtang boat, leave Radiwan Port early in the morning and do not miss the return boat, which usually leaves around 1-2 PM (confirm locally).
Prepare cash and offline maps. Outside Basco, ATMs and mobile signal are unreliable.

After seeing the house, walk around San Jose Church in Ivana town and the sea near Radiwan Port to see more of Ivatan daily life. The village is small and shops and restaurants are few, so bring water and snacks.
The House of Dakay is not a museum but a home where people live, so you must respect visiting hours, fees and photography rules, and not take away souvenirs, stones or roof grass.
The structures inside are old, so do not lean on or climb them. Watch your head where the ceiling is low.
Visit rules, registration places and fees differ by source. Check with your lodging or the tourism office before you go.
In typhoon season roads close and boats may be cancelled. Leave slack days for small-plane cancellations.
There are reports that Batanes visitor rules, including pre-registration, are changing, so check official announcements before you leave.
The year the house was built and the name of its builder differ by source, so they are hard to state with certainty. Follow the sign and the owner's explanation.
An island famous for its Ivatan stone-house villages, reached by boat from Radiwan Port in Ivana. You can compare its architecture with the House of Dakay.
A cliff viewpoint on the western sea in the Mahatao section. It is a good first stop in the morning of a full-day South Batan route.
A church in Ivana town that one trip report visited on its afternoon route. You can see the atmosphere of an Ivatan village.
Described as an unmanned shop that is said to be always open, though no official hours are confirmed. Follow the prices and the method.
An overview of all of Batanes, with its rolling grassy hills, stone-house villages and lighthouses. Check it first when planning your itinerary.
